page_title: How to Work Through Hard Math Problems

summary.title: How to Work Through Hard Math Problems
summary.one_liner: Learn a set of practical strategies, from trying something to returning to a problem later, for handling difficult math problems and the frustration that comes with them.
keywords: when to give up on a problem
feynman keep problems active in mind
takeaways: Difficult problems are worth engaging with; frustration often precedes key insights, and an easy problem set teaches less.
Start trying approaches even when unsure; most attempts fail, but they can prepare the mind for the right idea.
Useful tactics include simplifying the problem, working backwards, asking what hasn't been used yet, and reflecting on how past problems were solved.
Set a time limit, then read the solution actively: find the clues that pointed to it, and revisit the problem weeks later.
Ask for help early and start long assignments early, since prior thinking time makes complex ideas easier to grasp.
summary.summary: An essay from the Art of Problem Solving site responding to a student's frustration with hard problems. It argues that difficult problems train research-style thinking and general problem-solving, and that struggle is necessary for insight. The author then lists strategies such as doing something, simplifying, reflecting on past successes, focusing on unused information, working backwards, asking for help, starting early, taking breaks, starting over, giving up with a time limit, reading solutions actively, and returning to problems later, with personal anecdotes and a closing note on Feynman's habit of keeping problems active in his mind.
